help.polling:
Connect Slack, checking for messages

1. api.slack.com/apps › Create New App › From scratch. Name it Munder Difflin and pick your workspace.
2. OAuth & Permissions › Bot Token Scopes: add channels:history, groups:history, chat:write and files:read. Install to workspace.
3. Copy the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb) into the Bot token field here, and the channel id into Channel.
4. Invite the bot to that channel: /invite @MunderDifflin
5. Press Test connection, then Turn on. No Event Subscriptions, no Request URL.
help.socket:
Connect Slack, staying connected

1. api.slack.com/apps › Create New App › From scratch. Name it Munder Difflin and pick your workspace.
2. OAuth & Permissions › Bot Token Scopes: add channels:history, groups:history, chat:write and files:read. Install to workspace and copy the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb) into Bot token here.
3. Socket Mode › Enable Socket Mode. Basic Information › App Level Tokens › Generate, scope connections:write. Copy the token (xapp) into App token here.
4. Event Subscriptions › Enable Events › Subscribe to bot events: add message.channels and message.groups. No Request URL is needed. Save, reinstall if Slack asks.
5. Invite the bot to the channel: /invite @MunderDifflin, put the channel id in Channel, press Test connection, then Turn on.
help.webhook:
Connect Slack, letting Slack call the office

1. api.slack.com/apps › Create New App › From scratch. Name it Munder Difflin and pick your workspace.
2. Basic Information › Signing Secret: copy it into the Signing secret field here.
3. OAuth & Permissions › Bot Token Scopes: add chat:write, channels:history and groups:history. Install to workspace, then copy the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb) into the Bot token field here.
4. Press start below to launch the webhook and get your Request URL.
5. Event Subscriptions › Enable Events › Request URL: paste the Request URL from here and wait for Slack's green check.
6. Event Subscriptions › Subscribe to bot events: add message.channels and message.groups.
7. Event Subscriptions › Subscribe to events on behalf of users (add the matching user token scopes channels:history and groups:history first if Slack asks): add message.channels and message.groups.
8. Save Changes, reinstall if Slack prompts, then invite the bot to your channel: /invite @MunderDifflin

The Request URL changes on every start, so paste it again after a restart.

slack.steps:
Quickest: make the app from the manifest.
1. Press Copy manifest above.
2. api.slack.com/apps › Create New App › From a manifest. Pick your workspace, paste the manifest, then Next and Create.
3. Install App › Install to Workspace › Allow. Copy the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb) into Bot token.
4. Basic Information › App Level Tokens › Generate Token and Scopes: add connections:write, then Generate. Copy the token (xapp) into App token. Check every so often does not need it.
5. In Slack, type /invite @{{handle}} in each channel it should answer in. People can also message it directly. Press Test connection, then Save.

Slack walks you through steps instead? At "What it can respond to in Slack?" add the bot events {{events}}.

Made the app by hand? It needs the bot scopes {{scopes}}. Automatic and Live also need Socket Mode on, the bot events {{events}} under Event Subscriptions › Subscribe to bot events, and App Home › Messages Tab on with messages allowed. Reinstall the app after any change. Check every so often needs no events.

titles.homePlain: STEP 1 OF 4 · A HOME FOR THE APP

persona.headline: A CLONE OF YOU, WORKING 24/7
persona.body: Munder Difflin turns the CLI agent you already use into a clone of you — one that runs an office of long-running agents and keeps working while you're away. It manages everything around them: context, memory, tasks, triggers, environment, files, and integrations.
persona.ask: FIRST — WHO ARE YOU? (we'll tailor the setup)
persona.technicalDesc: I write code or work in a terminal. Show me CLI commands, flags, and model ids.
persona.nonTechnicalDesc: I'm in marketing, sales, ops, or just starting out. Explain things in plain language.

welcome.headline: YOUR CLONE AND THE FLOOR IT RUNS
welcome.descPlain: Your clone runs a small office of AI agents, and you watch it all from one screen. Here's what's inside:
welcome.desc: Your clone coordinates a hive of AI coding agents — persistent, watchable, all local. Here's what's inside:

engines.label: ELEVEN ENGINES, ONE OFFICE
engines.desc: Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Kimi, Antigravity, Qwen, OpenCode, Crush, pi, Copilot & Cursor — live agents on one floor.
engines.descPlain: Eleven AI assistants — Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Grok and more — working side by side in one shared office.

clone.label: {{godName}} IS YOUR CLONE
clone.desc: Your clone runs the floor — triages requests, routes tasks, and escalates only what needs you.
clone.descPlain: Your clone, {{godName}}, takes your requests, hands work to the right agent, and only interrupts you when it matters.

memory.label: LONG-TERM MEMORY
memory.desc: Each agent keeps notes, mined into a shared, searchable MemPalace.
memory.descPlain: Agents remember what they've done, so they don't start from scratch every time.

commandCenter.label: COMMAND CENTER
commandCenter.desc: Terminal · Floor · Memory · Activity · Tasks · Triggers in one control surface.
commandCenter.descPlain: One dashboard to watch the work, the agents' memory, tasks, and triggers.

guardrails.label: GUARDRAILS
guardrails.desc: Per-agent token budgets, a steer→constrain→stop circuit breaker, and human approvals.
guardrails.descPlain: Spending limits and safety stops keep agents in check — and they can ask you before big actions.

hires.label: READY-MADE HIRES
hires.desc: Grab a pre-configured agent from the Agent Gallery and spawn it in one click.
hires.descPlain: Hire a ready-made agent from the gallery in one click — no setup needed.

providerBlurb.qwen: Qwen — runs a local Qwen model on your machine
providerBlurb.cursor: Cursor Agent CLI — uses your Cursor credits (Luna, Composer, …)

home.descPlain: Create a new, empty folder for the app to call home. Everything the app remembers — its own settings and your agents' memory — is stored here. Something like ~/HarnessAgents works well. We'll create it for you if it doesn't exist.
home.desc: Pick a folder where the harness will keep its own files — agent metadata, logs, and any new repos you create from here. Something like ~/HarnessAgents is a fine default. We'll create it if it doesn't exist.
home.notePlain: You won't need to open this folder day-to-day — it's just where the app keeps its notes so nothing is lost when you restart.
home.note: Think of this as the "town hall." The harness pins agent state there so sessions can be picked back up after a restart.

orchestrator.descPlain: {{godName}} is your clone — he reads your requests, breaks them into tasks, and hands them to the right agent. He's the boss of the floor; you're still the boss of him. Choose which AI engine powers him.
orchestrator.desc: {{godName}} is your clone — the boss of the floor you just met. He triages your requests, assigns tasks, and manages the team, while escalating anything that genuinely needs you. Pick the engine and model that power him; give him a longer-context, higher-capability model.
orchestrator.cliAgentPlain: A CLI agent is an AI coding assistant that runs on your computer — popular ones are Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI) and Antigravity (Google Gemini). Your clone is the always-on one that runs your whole office. We recommend Claude Code on Opus 4.8 (1M). You can add or switch the others later.
orchestrator.cliAgent: Each option is a CLI engine (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity/Gemini, or a local proxy like Qwen). Engines marked INSTALLED are already on this machine; INSTALLS ON FIRST RUN means the app sets it up when {{godName}} first starts. Your clone ({{godName}}) is the engine that orchestrates the whole hive. Recommended: Claude Code · Opus 4.8 · 1M. Other providers can be wired per agent later.
orchestrator.workersOnlyHint: Cannot drain hive mail yet, so it cannot run your clone. Still available when hiring temps.
orchestrator.modelNote: This only sets {{godName}}'s engine. You can run other providers per agent later.

repos.descPlain: Add your projects. A project is simply a folder — it can hold code, documents, notes, or any files you want your agents to work with. You can create a brand-new folder or pick an existing one, and add more anytime.
repos.desc: Add the repos you want your agents to work in. Each folder becomes a project (a room on the floor) — multiple agents can share one. You can add more later.
repos.emptyPlain: No projects added yet. Optional — you can add one later.
repos.empty: No repos added yet. Optional, but recommended.

permissions.autonomyHead: HOW MUCH CAN AGENTS DO ON THEIR OWN?
permissions.autoLabelPlain: LET AGENTS WORK ON THEIR OWN
permissions.autoOnPlain: On. Agents carry out tasks without stopping to ask — the smoothest experience.
permissions.autoOffPlain: Off. Agents pause and ask you before changing files or running commands.
permissions.autoOn: On. Agents never pause — Claude runs bypassPermissions, Codex bypasses approvals + sandbox, etc.
permissions.autoOff: Off. Each agent asks before edits / shell commands (Claude default, codex -a untrusted, …).
permissions.autoNotePlain: Best when agents work in their own projects. You can change this later, including for individual agents.
permissions.autoNote: The right default for the "control room" experience; a foot-gun on production repos. Override per agent in the Add Agent dialog.
permissions.reliabilityHead: KEEP THINGS RUNNING WHILE YOU'RE AWAY
permissions.reliabilityDescPlain: Your agents keep working on a schedule and in live terminals, even when you step away. These settings keep you in the loop and keep things running.
permissions.reliabilityDesc: Your agents keep working on a schedule and in live terminals. If your computer fully sleeps those timers pause and catch up the moment you're back — nothing is lost, it may just run late.
permissions.keepAwakeDesc: Strong keep-alive: stops your computer from sleeping while an agent is live, so schedules and terminals fire on time even when you step away. Uses more battery — best on power. Off by default.
permissions.notificationsDesc: Get pinged when an agent needs you or a terminal needs reviving — even while you're away. Your system may ask permission the first time one fires.
permissions.openAtLoginDesc: Relaunch the harness after a reboot so scheduled missions resume on their own. No prompt — applies immediately.
permissions.stayAwakeDescMac: macOS only lets you set this one yourself. In Battery → Options, turn on "Prevent automatic sleeping when the display is off" (on power adapter) so timers keep firing with the display asleep. Without a sleep-preventing setting the Mac still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.
permissions.stayAwakeDescWindows: Windows only lets you set this one yourself. In Settings → System → Power & battery → Screen, blank & sleep, set "On battery power, put my device to sleep" and "When plugged in" to Never (or increase them) so timers keep firing. Without a sleep-preventing setting Windows still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.
permissions.stayAwakeDescLinux: Your desktop environment only lets you set this one yourself. Look for a Power Settings panel (e.g. GNOME Settings → Power, or KDE System Settings → Power Management) and disable automatic sleep/suspend while on power. Without a sleep-preventing setting your machine still truly sleeps — work survives and catches up on wake.

contextSection.intro: Compact runs when an agent's turn ends with its context at or over the bar. An engine that reports no token count is compacted on the timer instead. Clear runs on its timer, once the context is at least as full as its bar. A bar of 0% means the timer alone.
contextSection.compactBlurb: Summarises the context so the thread keeps going.
contextSection.clearBlurb: Discards the context. Nothing is summarised.
contextSection.clearCaution: Clearing throws context away — it is not a smaller version of compaction. An agent mid-task forgets what it was doing. Leave this off unless you keep context another way.
contextSection.extraFocusHint: Appended to the provider's compaction command. Empty sends the bare command.
contextSection.commandHint: Sent literally. Empty sends the bare clear command.
contextSection.contextBarHint: How full the window must be before this may run. 0% = time alone.
contextSection.bigWindowsHint: Used on ~1M-token windows, where a smaller slice is still an enormous amount of text.
contextSection.hintCompact: When a turn ends at {{pct}}% ({{tokens}} tokens), or {{large}}% ({{largeTokens}} tokens) on a 1M window.

contextSection.fallbackEveryHint: An agent that reports a token count does not wait for this. It is compacted when its turn ends at the bar.
contextSection.compactBarHint: The compact runs when a turn ends at that size.
contextSection.switchClear: Clear on a switch of work
contextSection.switchClearBlurb: When an agent is woken for other work than it is on, and its session is old enough, it writes its handoff, its context is cleared, and then it gets the new work.

conn.label: Label
conn.secretKeep: A key is saved. Leave blank to keep it, or paste a new one to replace it.
conn.errUrl: The base URL must start with https:// (or http://localhost).
conn.errHeader: The header name may hold letters, digits and hyphens only.

authWhy.none: Nothing is added to the request. For an API that needs no key.
authWhy.bearer: Sends Authorization: Bearer and your key. The most common shape; Stripe, Notion and Sentry use it.
authWhy.header: Sends your key on its own under a header you name. Pick this when the docs show a header with no word in front of the key. If the docs give you an id and a secret, pick HTTP basic instead.
authWhy.prefix: Sends a word and then your key under a header you name. Pick this when the docs show Token, ApiKey or SSWS in front of it.
authWhy.query: Sends your key as a query parameter on every URL. Common on weather, news and maps APIs.
authWhy.basic: Sends a user and your key as HTTP basic. Atlassian, Twilio and Mailgun take an email and a token this way.
authWhy.github: Sends Authorization: Bearer and your token, with the two headers the GitHub REST API expects.

conn.headerHint: The header name from your provider's docs. Letters, digits and hyphens.
conn.prefixHint: One word. The space before your key is added for you.
conn.paramHint: The parameter name from your provider's docs.
conn.userHint: The left half of the pair, usually an email. Your key is the right half and stays in the encrypted store.
conn.probeHint: Optional. A read only path under the base URL that Test calls, such as plans?count=1. Leave blank to test the base URL itself.
conn.keyRejected: Key rejected ({{status}}). Check the key and, for HTTP basic, the user.
conn.pathNotFound: Reached the service, but the test path was not found (404). Set a Test path to check the key.
conn.sendsNothing: Nothing is added to the request.
conn.sendsMasked: The stars stand where your key goes. The key itself is never shown again.
conn.errPrefix: The prefix is one word of letters, digits or hyphens.
conn.errParam: The parameter name may hold letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens only.
conn.errUser: Give the user for the pair, without a colon.
conn.errDuplicate: A connection already uses that id. Change the label.

responseStyle.title: Response style
responseStyle.desc: The brief every agent works under when it answers. It reaches all six engines.
responseStyle.label: Style brief

responseStyle.claudeStyleDesc: Claude Code has an output style setting of its own. Agents started here use Concise, which saves tokens. Every other engine gets the brief above instead.
responseStyle.claudeStyleApplies: Applies the next time an agent starts or restarts.
responseStyle.reach: Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok pick this up on their very next turn. Cursor and Copilot pick it up on the next message the app sends them.

newFloor.title: NEW FLOOR: WHERE TO START?
newFloor.blurb: A floor is one hive in its own window and its own process. Pick a folder that holds a hive, or a new folder and the app lays a fresh hive inside it. The hive this window is on stays here; a hive that is open in another floor cannot be opened twice.
newFloor.errCurrent: That folder is the hive this floor is already on.
newFloor.errHeld: That folder is open in another floor (pid {{pid}}). Close that floor first, or pick another folder.
newFloor.errSameData: A floor cannot use this floor's own data folder.
newFloor.errInvalid: That is not a folder this app can open.
newFloor.errNoSpawner: Opening a hive in its own floor is not in this build yet. The picker and the lock are; the process per floor lands next.
newFloor.errSpawn: The new floor did not start: {{detail}}

quitWarning.title: QUITTING NOW?
quitWarning.killBody: Kill all & quit ends every running agent session at once. Anything an agent was holding in memory and had not yet saved is lost.
quitWarning.killKeeps: Everything already saved stays: tasks, memory, files, and the conversation records on disk. The app then closes.
